title: Saudis Shut East-West Pipeline After Drones From Iraq Strike Hormuz Bypass as Modi Hosts Putin, Xi and Iran at BRICS
subhead: A drone attack launched from Iraqi territory forced Saudi Arabia to shutter the East-West Pipeline — the main overland bypass for Hormuz traffic — while Houthis seized Perim Island to complete their grip on Bab al-Mandab. Energy lines from the Gulf are being cut one by one even as leaders gather in India for a BRICS summit shadowed by two wars.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Shuts Its Hormuz-Bypass Pipeline After Iraq-Launched Drone Strikes
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia shut down the East-West Pipeline — the roughly 1,200-km line that carries crude from the Gulf coast to the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz — after multiple drones launched from Iraqi territory struck it, triggering fires and reported injuries. Reuters reported Riyadh is holding off on retaliation even as it condemned the attack; the Gulf Cooperation Council issued its strongest condemnation. In a sign of the strain the episode places on Baghdad, Reuters and Middle East Eye reported that Iraq's prime minister dismissed a senior military commander in the wake of the drone strikes and ordered a probe.

The strategic weight of the strike is hard to overstate: with Hormuz effectively shut and the Red Sea route increasingly contested, the East-West Pipeline was one of the last remaining overland alternatives for Gulf crude. Knocking it out closes an artery that had become more valuable precisely because sea lanes are failing. Al Jazeera cited satellite imagery showing damage to the pipeline. The attack also opens a new and diplomatically awkward front — for the first time, Gulf territory is being hit from Iraqi soil, complicating the US-Iraq relationship even as Baghdad had declared a September 30 US withdrawal 'final'.
sections.whyItMatters: Removing the main land-based Hormuz bypass, on top of Houthi pressure on the Red Sea, tightens the squeeze on global oil supply from two directions at once — and thrusts Iraq into the center of an escalation it had tried to stay out of.

sections.heading: Houthis Seize Perim Island, Tightening Their Grip on Bab al-Mandab
sections.body:
The Houthis consolidated their hold on the southern Red Sea this week, capturing Perim Island — the rocky outcrop that controls the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait through which much of the world's container and tanker traffic passes. Multiple outlets, including AP, the New York Times and the Times of Israel, reported Yemeni government forces withdrew from Perim as Houthi fighters closed in, following their earlier seizure of Mokha and Mayyun Island. Iranian media claimed the Houthis now effectively control the strait, a claim contested but underscored by the group's documented advance along Yemen's Red Sea coast.

This is not just another Red Sea skirmish. Perim and Mayyun bracket Bab al-Mandab at its narrowest point, giving whoever holds them the ability to monitor and interdict shipping through the key link between the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Combined with the Saudi pipeline shutdown, the Houthis are closing the strategic pincer around Gulf energy exports from the south at the same moment Iraq threatens them from the north.
sections.whyItMatters: Control of Bab al-Mandab's gateway islands converts Houthi harassment into a structural stranglehold on one of the world's two most important oil chokepoints, compounding the Hormuz crisis and pushing a growing share of global trade onto longer, costlier routings.

sections.heading: Anthropic Says Iran-Linked Actors Used Its Claude AI to Target US Navy Ships
sections.body:
AI company Anthropic disclosed that accounts linked to Iran used its Claude model to compile targeting data on US Navy warships operating in the Middle East, according to the Wall Street Journal, Reuters and Navy Times. The company said Iranian, Houthi, Russian and Chinese-linked actors also used Claude in attempts to develop weapons, conduct cyber operations and run propaganda and influence campaigns. Iran International and Al-Monitor reported the activity included targeting guides on US naval assets and, in Yemen, missile and influence projects.

The disclosure matters less for what one model can do than for what it reveals about the new terrain of conflict. Off-the-shelf frontier AI is now a dual-use accelerant that hostile state and proxy networks can weaponize for targeting, disinformation and weapons development — capabilities that previously required dedicated state programs. This is a first, public, named case of an American AI model being turned against American military forces, and it will sharpen debates in Washington and Brussels about export controls and model-safety thresholds.
sections.whyItMatters: If Iranian-linked cells can build US naval targeting guides from a widely available commercial AI, then the barrier to AI-enabled targeting has collapsed — a shift with direct implications for how navies operate in contested waters and how democracies regulate frontier models.

sections.heading: Modi Hosts Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian for an 11-Nation BRICS Summit Shadowed by War
sections.body:
Russia's Vladimir Putin, China's Xi Jinping and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian converged in India for a BRICS summit of eleven members, in what Al Jazeera described as a gathering clouded by both the Ukraine and Iran wars. Reuters reported Modi stressed the need to protect navigation and seafarers in talks with Pezeshkian — a pointed message as Iran-backed forces threaten shipping lanes — while AP noted Modi also held talks with Putin ahead of the summit. The New York Times framed the expansion as evidence that emerging powers keep joining BRICS even when they sharply disagree with one another.

The meeting is a study in strategic straddling. India hosts the leaders of states actively at odds with Washington, yet New Delhi's own security depends on the same shipping lanes the Iran-aligned axis is endangering. Modi's navigation message to Pezeshkian signals India is trying to hold the bloc to a rule-based norm on maritime traffic even as it deepens trade ties with Tehran. BRICS is becoming a venue where the non-Western majority gathers — but its members' divergent interests, visible in this very summit, limit how far it can function as a coherent counterweight.
sections.whyItMatters: The simultaneous presence of Moscow, Beijing and Tehran in New Delhi shows the anti-Western bloc has staying power, but India's open pushback on maritime security exposes the internal fault lines that prevent BRICS from acting as a unified bloc on the crises of the day.

sections.heading: Oil Above $100 as Nuclear Files Move in Vienna: IAEA Sends Iran to UNSC, Flags New North Korea Plant
sections.body:
The energy and nuclear frontlines moved in parallel this week. Brent crude settled up more than $4 a barrel, climbing back above $100 as renewed US-Iran fighting and tight supply bit, with diesel prices at record highs and Pakistan's pump prices crossing 400 rupees a litre, according to Fortune, AP and Reuters. Meanwhile the IAEA board referred Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years over non-compliance, as AP and Al Jazeera reported, and the watchdog flagged a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility at North Korea's Yongbyon site — a development Reuters said could add several warheads' worth of fissile material a year.

The two nuclear stories are separately significant but jointly unsettling. Iran's referral to the Security Council reopens a UN track that has been dormant for two decades, with unclear enforcement prospects at a moment the US is already at war with Tehran. North Korea's new enrichment plant indicates Pyongyang is quietly expanding its fissile capacity despite its isolation and its missile-test pace. Both advance the underlying reality: the non-proliferation framework is being tested in parallel to, and partly because of, the wars consuming the world's attention.
sections.whyItMatters: Energy above $100 and simultaneous nuclear escalations in Iran and North Korea show the costs of the Middle East war are compounding even as the atomic files that preceded it resurface — a reminder that today's conflicts rest on unresolved proliferation and supply vulnerabilities.

bottomLine: The defining development of the day is that the Gulf's energy escape routes are disappearing in parallel: a drone attack launched from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to shut the East-West Pipeline, the key overland Hormuz bypass, even as Houthis seized Perim Island to complete their hold on Bab al-Mandab. With both sea lanes and the main land alternative now compromised, oil is climbing back above $100 and the squeeze on global supply is tightening from every direction. Add Iraq's emergence as a launch point for strikes against Gulf territory, Iran-linked actors using commercial AI to target US warships, and the concentration of Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian under one roof in India — and the picture is of a conflict that is widening in geography, technology and participation rather than de-escalating. The wars are no longer contained to their original theaters, and each day's escalation raises both the energy cost and the difficulty of finding an off-ramp.
